title: What all share: ethics and practice
hook: precepts, meditation and kindness run through every school

segments.voice: Yesterday, the three jewels: the Buddha, the dhamma and the sangha, the refuge the schools hold in common. Your line was three jewels for all. Where did one of the three show up in your day? Day one thousand three hundred sixty-two.

Three robes at one breakfast table. Saffron, from a forest monastery in Thailand. Black, from a Zen temple in Japan. Maroon, from a Tibetan nunnery. Ask each of them how the morning went. One chanted the precepts in Pali before dawn. One sat facing a white wall until the bell. One recited verses wishing every being well. Three languages, three rooms, three very different mornings. And yet if you listen a little longer, you can pick out three threads running through all of them: a promise about how to act, a time for training the mind, and a wish for other people's good. Today, the ground under all three chairs.
screen: `SAFFRON, BLACK, MAROON.` → `THREE MORNINGS.` → `THE SAME THREE THREADS.`

segments.voice: First, conduct. The Pali word is sila. For lay Buddhists it takes the shape of the five precepts: no killing, no stealing, no sexual misconduct, no false speech, and no intoxicants that cloud the mind. Notice how they're said. Not as commandments handed down, but as training rules a person takes on: I undertake to train in this. The promise is yours. Monks and nuns keep far more rules, and some Mahayana communities add bodhisattva precepts on top. But the five are the ground floor. Second, training the mind. Here the schools look very different. Noting the rise and fall of the belly in Burma. Zazen in Japan. Visualizing a Buddha in Tibet. Walking slowly in a Korean courtyard. Chanting a name in a Chinese hall. The outward shapes vary a great deal. What runs underneath is the same work: steadying attention so it can see clearly. Third, kindness. Theravada homes chant the discourse on loving-kindness, metta. Mahayana temples speak of great compassion, the wish to free all beings. Different words, and both are wishes spoken for other people's good. And fourth, one verse that gathers all of it. The Dhammapada, in Max Müller's translation, says: "Not to commit any sin, to do good, and to purify one's mind, that is the teaching of (all) the Awakened." Don't harm. Do good. Train the heart. Conduct, kindness, mind. A Thai monk, a Japanese priest and a Tibetan nun could each recite their own version of that line, and mean it.
screen: `SILA: PRECEPTS TAKEN ON, NOT IMPOSED.` · `MANY SHAPES OF MEDITATION.` · `METTA AND GREAT COMPASSION.` · `NOT TO HARM, TO DO GOOD, TO PURIFY.` · then, large: `THE COMMON GROUND.`

segments.voice: If you'd like, take one precept for today. Sit comfortably and let a few breaths come and go. Then look at the five: not harming, not taking what isn't given, care in desire, honest speech, a clear mind. Which one would actually stretch you today? Choose just that one. Hold it in plain words, the way the old formula does: I'll train in this today. Then rest with your breath, and let the promise sit there quietly beside it. The bell holds the time.
What all share. Beneath the robes and the languages: precepts, a trained mind and kindness, running underneath the schools we've met this year. Today's word.
Your line: the common ground. Today, keep the one precept you chose, and notice one moment when it asks something of you. Day one thousand three hundred sixty-two.

howItsDone: Lay Buddhists in Theravada, Mahayana and Vajrayana communities often recite the five precepts as training rules they take on, alongside meditation and chanting for the good of all beings.

notes: Confirm the exact Müller 1881 wording of Dhammapada 183, including the parenthetical '(all)'.

The five precepts are listed as commonly recited by lay Buddhists in many lands; the count is the precepts' own. Confirm the plain-English wording of each, especially 'sexual misconduct' and 'intoxicants that cloud the mind'.

Meditation forms tied to countries (breath counting in Burma, zazen in Japan, visualization in Tibet, walking in Korea, name-chanting in China) are illustrative, not exclusive; confirm the pairings are fair.
Trapdoor: the threefold training (sila, samadhi, panna) attributed to the Pali suttas; confirm phrasing.
